extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of science, philosophers of mathematics, advanced students and researchers interested in the nature of mathematical explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and analysis of what counts as an explanation when mathematics is involved, both in empirical sciences and within mathematics itself, comparing accounts (law-based, causal/mechanistic, counterfactual, structural, model-based, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation requires causes (Aristotelian/causal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Aristotelian and many contemporary accounts, explanations require causes or causal information; demonstrating the cause yields scientific knowledge (e.g. Aristotle: demonstrative understanding depends on premises that are explanatory of the conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion supports mechanistic/causal accounts (Salmon, new mechanists). Anti-pattern: treating mathematical connections as explanations when they merely relate truths without providing causal mechanisms (e.g. objections to Newtonian mathematical treatments that lack physical mechanisms). Example guidance: prefer demonstrations that mirror causal structure when the aim is causal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-based/deductive-nomological requirement (Hempel/Kitcher style)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation is a deductively valid argument from true premises where at least one premise is a scientific law (Hempel); Kitcher emphasizes unifying deductive argument schemes identified by global features of accepted claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when assessing explanations that appeal to laws or unification. Examples: Hempel-style proofs; Kitcher-style unifying argument schemes. Anti-pattern: counting explanatory arguments that lack law-like premises as Hempel-style explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic explanation / explanation as mechanism (new mechanists, Salmon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations are identified with causal mechanisms or processes that produce the explanandum; showcasing the mechanism counts as an explanation even without law-based deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an account specifies entities, activities, and organization that generate the phenomenon. Anti-patterns: labeling abstract mathematical relations as mechanisms without linking to production of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual / interventionist difference-making requirement (Lewis, Woodward)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation indicates how changes (counterfactuals or interventions) in factors would make a difference to the explanandum; explanations are about difference-making relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterfactual tests or interventionist analysis to judge explanatory relevance. Guidance notes discuss how these accounts can be extended to non-causal mathematical cases but face challenges (which counterfactuals count, asymmetry objections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for non-causal mathematical explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics can play an explanatory role without representing causes (e.g. impossibility explanations like divisibility, structural/topological explanations such as Königsberg bridges, optimality/minimization explanations like cicada prime years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize explanatory value even when no causal relation is invoked. Examples: divisibility explains impossibility of equal sharing; graph-theoretic structure explains bridging impossibility; prime-number arguments explain cicada cycles. Anti-pattern: insisting all explanations must be causal and thereby dismissing such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal/necessity-based explanatory power (Lange: explanations by constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical claims can explain by virtue of their special modal strength or necessity; claims with appropriate modal character (necessity) can constrain what is possible and thus explain outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a mathematical claim has sufficient modal force to guarantee or constrain outcomes (e.g. 9×9=81 guarantees possibility of arranging 81 stamps). Beware of overgeneration: modal necessity alone may count too many things as explanatory unless supplemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countermathematical / impossible-worlds tests for mathematical explanation (Baron, Povich, Baron et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematical claims like causes by assessing counterfactuals in impossible worlds (where necessary truths are false) to see if altering the mathematical claim would change the explanandum; requires careful treatment of impossible worlds and their epistemic access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying, ensure the impossible-world scenario is 'just enough' change and that natural-world features implicated in the mathematics are correspondingly changed (Baron et al.). Anti-pattern: naive counterfactual substitution that ignores required natural-world adjustments (stamp example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional requirements beyond counterfactuals for distinctively mathematical explanations (Baron/Kitcher style concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Baron and others argue that passing a countermathematical test is not sufficient to identify genuinely mathematical explanations; additional constraints like unification or special argument schemes may be required to distinguish tracking from genuine mathematical explanatory work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for features that make the mathematics explanatorily distinctive (e.g. unification, novel insight) rather than merely restating non-mathematical facts. Anti-pattern: counting trivial representational matches (9×9=81 tracking the stamp count) as distinctively mathematical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program explanation / indispensability to a program (Lyon)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation is mathematical when it functions as a 'program explanation' that uses mathematics indispensably to guarantee the presence of some member of a family of properties, one of which is causally relevant to the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the mathematics is indispensable to the program that secures the causal property. Anti-pattern: cases where mathematics only represents causally relevant properties but is not indispensable to the explanatory program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/ontic structural realism criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the world's fundamental metaphysical structure is identified with mathematical structure, then mathematical structures provide direct explanatory resources—mathematical explanations become natural if science is about those structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an ontological interpretive move: adopt only if willing to accept strong metaphysical commitments (structural realism). Use when evaluating explanations in fundamental physics where mathematical structure plausibly is the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models can explain despite falsehoods (models-and-idealization criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific models need not be literally true to explain; models explain when they generate some truths about their target via representation or inferential licenses even if they contain false idealizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the model represents relevant features of the target and yields true claims about it. Anti-pattern: dismissing explanatory value simply because a model idealizes (e.g. infinitely deep ocean) — instead examine which aspects are representationally responsible for the explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-target representation / inferential license requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A model explains only when there is a representation relation or an agent-established inferential license that legitimately connects model claims to truths about the target system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether structural relations, conventions, or inferential rules have been established to map model elements to target features. Anti-pattern: assuming structural isomorphism is necessary or sufficient for representation; structural relation can be neither necessary nor sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical-operations/limit-based explanations (Batterman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematical explanations rely essentially on mathematical operations (e.g. taking limits, thermodynamic limit) that connect models and produce idealizations that are explanatorily indispensable without themselves representing the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize operations that transform one model into another can be the explanans; evaluate whether the idealization introduced by the operation is essential (not merely removable by a Galilean idealization). Example: universality in phase transitions via thermodynamic limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory indispensability argument for mathematical ontology (Colyvan/Baker)
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematical entities are indispensable to our best scientific theories (especially for explanation), then we have ontological reason to be committed to those entities (platonist conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ontological commitment, examine whether mathematics is genuinely indispensable to explanation (not merely convenient or reformulable). Consider responses that contest indispensability or propose nominalist strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory pluralism (distinct kinds of explanation allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations may come in a plurality of distinct sorts (causal, non-causal, topological, programmatic, model-based), and no single account may cover all cases; the value of explanation often ties to scientific understanding produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt pluralist stance when encountering diverse explanatory practices; evaluate explanations relative to the kind they instantiate. Anti-pattern: forcing all explanations into a single monistic framework and thereby excluding legitimate non-causal mathematical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological/structural explanation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Topological or network-based features (structural properties) can serve as non-causal explanations by showing how structural constraints or relations account for phenomena (e.g. some explanations in epidemiology, connectivity, or phase space features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the structural feature is explanatorily relevant and not merely descriptive. Consider whether such explanations can be reduced to mechanisms or must be treated as a distinct explanatory kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that explanations deliver understanding (epistemic value)
rubrics_metrics.description: One aim of explanations is to produce scientific understanding; accounts must make sense of why grasping an explanation is valuable even across different kinds of explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate explanations also by their capacity to increase understanding (grasping, unification, insight). Consider debates about what constitutes understanding and whether different accounts capture its value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry and counterfactual test limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfactual accounts face challenges such as explanatory asymmetry (why some counterfactual relations seem symmetric but explanatory relations are asymmetric) and selecting appropriate counterfactuals for mathematical cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing counterfactual tests, check for asymmetry issues and whether the chosen counterfactuals legitimately track explanatory direction. Anti-pattern: treating every true counterfactual implication as evidence of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation vs. non-representational explanatory roles of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish explanations where mathematics represents explanatorily relevant factors (causes, difference-makers) from cases where mathematics plays an expressive or structural role without straightforward representation (e.g. Batterman-style idealizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and evaluate mathematical contributions accordingly: representational explanations require mapping/modeling; non-representational ones may rely on operations, limits, or structural identification. Anti-pattern: conflating representation with all explanatory roles of mathematics.
